summary: A 1970 specification for network use of the UCSB On-Line System. It was updated by RFC 217 and RFC 225.

eli5.summary: This note explains how others on the network could use an interactive computer system at one university.

questions: what is the ucsb on-line system
how did users log in to ucsb ols over the arpanet
what output classes did ols use
subtitle: How a program on another ARPANET host could log in to UCSB's Culler-Fried On-Line System through a small interface process.

tldr.problem: UCSB's On-Line System (OLS) was an interactive system built for local keyboards and display scopes, and remote Network users needed a defined way to send it keystrokes and receive its displays.
tldr.mechanism: An Interface process listens on socket x'101' at site 3, hands each user a pair of connections, passes input key codes straight to OLS, and relays OLS output as length-prefixed records in three classes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 74 is a programmer's guide to the Interface rather than a user's manual. The index lists it as updated by RFC 217 and RFC 225.

today: The RFC index lists this document as updated by RFC 217 and RFC 225, and its status is recorded as unknown. It describes a single 1970 system and the Host-Host protocol of that time.

sections.title: The On-Line System as a Network Service
sections.content:
RFC 74 describes how Network users reach UCSB's On-Line System (OLS), which is available as socket number x'101' at site 3. Users log in with OLS account parameters that the RFC lists, using the site name (UCLA, SRI, UTAH, BBN, MIT, SDC or RAND) as the user name.

Users do not talk to OLS directly. They talk to an intermediary process called the Interface, which works through the Host-Host protocol of 3 August 70 and the NCP and is reached through the Logger. The document is meant for programmers and is explicitly not a user's manual for OLS. Both sides treat the first message as Type 0: the first eight bits are zeros, and after that Imp-message boundaries do not matter.
sections.eli5: This note is the instruction sheet for the doorman of a computer clubhouse. It tells programmers how to talk to him, not how to play the games inside.

sections.title: Logging In Through the Interface
sections.content:
The Interface is in core only while at least one Network user is connected; otherwise it sits on direct-access storage and the Logger listens on the primary socket. The Logger rejects the first call, loads the Interface and starts it, so a user whose first request is rejected should simply ask again. A second rejection means OLS is inactive or that the Interface or the NCP has run out of resources.

Over the first connection the Interface sends eight bits of zeros and then a 32-bit socket number from its pool, closes the connection and listens again. It then requests two connections with the user: its local socket numbered as sent with the user's socket plus one, and its local socket plus one with the user's socket. These become the Input Connection and the Output Connection, which stay open until the user closes them.
sections.eli5: You knock on the front door. If the doorman is asleep, a helper wakes him and tells you to knock again. Then he hands you a number, closes the door, and sets up two private pipes with you: one for talking and one for listening.

sections.title: The Input Connection
sections.content:
After the first two bytes, input is a continuous stream of one-byte key codes. The Interface passes each one unexamined to OLS, which handles it exactly as if it came from a directly attached keyboard and discards invalid codes. The user should first log in to OLS and should finish by logging off (SYST DOWN), because otherwise a later Network user could find the session already logged in.

The first byte is discarded as the Type 0 byte. The second byte is read by the Interface and lets the user suppress classes of output: bit 0 set suppresses all alphanumeric output, bit 1 all curvilinear output and bit 2 all special character output. Bits 3 to 7 are not examined and should be zeros. The choice holds for the life of the connections and saves traffic the user could not display anyway.
sections.eli5: Everything you type goes straight through the pipe to the clubhouse. The very first thing you send is a little note saying which kinds of pictures you do not want, so they do not clog your pipe.

sections.title: Output Records and Their Three Classes
sections.content:
After a first byte of zeros, the Output Connection carries variable-length records. Each record has a one-byte output class, a one-byte class-dependent field, a data field, and a two-byte length of the data and class-dependent fields in bits. Only classes the user has enabled are sent, and the length of a record in bits is its length field plus twenty-four.

  • Class 1, alphameric: a string of one-byte characters such as the Greek and Latin letters and carriage controls. The pair BACK ERASE (x'59BC') erases the scope, and BREAK (x'79') means a carriage return on a scope with twenty-five characters per line but a space on a printer.
  • Class 2, curvilinear: a list of X-Y coordinates, each in two bytes, in line segment, dot or character mode. The display area is square with the origin at lower left and both X and Y running from 0 to 4095.
  • Class 3, special characters: moves in one of sixteen directions, or a four-byte change in position relative to the last character frame, which is 160 units wide and 224 units high.
sections.eli5: What comes back is a stream of small parcels. Each parcel says what kind of thing it is, how big it is, and then holds the letters, line drawings or little shapes to show on your screen.
